label: Shared responsibility across IaaS, PaaS and SaaS

mentor.diagnosis: You assigned a responsibility to the wrong party. The dividing line moves with the service model, and the exam picks the model deliberately.
mentor.rule: Your data, your accounts and your configuration are yours in every model, without exception. Everything else shifts to the provider as you move from IaaS toward SaaS.
mentor.tell: 'Who is responsible for patching the guest operating system' is IaaS only. A misconfigured storage bucket or an over-permissioned account is always the customer, whatever the model.
mentor.trap: SaaS feels like the provider handles everything, which is why public data exposure through a misconfigured SaaS permission is such a common real world breach. Configuration never transfers.

label: Hot, warm and cold recovery sites

mentor.diagnosis: You matched a site type to the wrong recovery time or cost. The three differ only by how much is already running when you arrive.
contrast: Hardware, software and current data, running
Hardware and software, data is stale or must be restored
mentor.rule: Hot means data is already there and current. Warm means the kit is there and the data is not. Cold means an empty room.
mentor.tell: Match to the RTO in the stem. An RTO of one hour rules out warm and cold immediately. A tight budget with a tolerant RTO points to cold.
mentor.trap: Warm sites are described as having hardware and software ready, which sounds nearly instant. The missing current data is what costs you the hours or days.

label: High availability, load balancing and clustering

mentor.diagnosis: You treated these as the same thing. They overlap and they solve different problems.
contrast: Spread requests across servers for capacity
Traffic is directed to the remaining nodes
Servers act as one logical system, sharing state
Another node takes over the workload and its state
Achieved by the above plus redundancy everywhere
mentor.rule: Load balancing is about capacity and gives availability as a side effect. Clustering is about servers acting as one system with shared state. High availability is the goal, not the mechanism.
mentor.tell: 'Distribute incoming requests across the web farm' is load balancing. 'The database must keep running with its session state intact if a node fails' is clustering.
mentor.trap: A load balancer does improve availability, so it answers many availability questions. When the stem stresses shared state or a single logical system, it is clustering.

label: Snapshot vs replication vs journaling vs backup

mentor.diagnosis: You chose a data protection method that does not survive the scenario's failure mode. Replication in particular is not a backup.
contrast: A separate copy retained over time
Deletion, corruption, ransomware, going back in time
A point in time view, usually on the same storage
Bad change or upgrade, recent and fast
A record of every change, so you can replay to any moment
Very small RPO, fine grained recovery
mentor.rule: Replication copies your mistakes as fast as it copies your data. Only a retained, separated backup lets you go back to before the damage.
mentor.tell: Ransomware or accidental deletion means backup, and it must be offline or immutable. Site loss means replication. Near zero RPO means journaling or continuous replication.
mentor.trap: Replication sounds strictly better than backup because it is continuous. Continuity is exactly the problem: the encryption or the deletion replicates too.

label: Data at rest, in transit and in use

mentor.diagnosis: You applied a protection that does not cover the state the data was actually in.
contrast: On disk, in a database, in object storage
Full disk, volume, database or field encryption
Secure enclave, confidential computing, homomorphic encryption
mentor.rule: Data in use is the hard one. It has to be decrypted to be processed, which is why it needs a hardware enclave rather than ordinary encryption.
mentor.tell: 'Protect the data even from the administrator of the server while the application is processing it' is data in use.
mentor.trap: Full disk encryption is the reflex answer and it protects a powered off device. Once the system is running and the volume is mounted, it protects nothing against a live attacker.

mentor.diagnosis: You answered with a classification level when the question asked what kind of data it is, or the reverse.
contrast: What kind of information is this
Regulated, trade secret, intellectual property, legal, financial, human readable
How sensitive is it to us
Public, private, sensitive, confidential, restricted, critical
A recipe is a trade secret
mentor.rule: Type describes the nature of the data and often who regulates it. Classification describes the handling level your organisation assigns.
mentor.tell: If the options are Public, Private, Confidential and Restricted, the question wants a classification. If they are Regulated, Trade secret and Intellectual property, it wants a type.
mentor.trap: Both axes appear in the same option list, so a word that sounds right is always available on the wrong axis. This is the same trick as control category versus control type.

mentor.diagnosis: You picked a connectivity technology when the requirement was security delivered with the connectivity, or the reverse.
contrast: Encrypted tunnel for a user or a site
Intelligent routing across multiple circuits between sites
Network and security delivered together from the cloud edge
Yes: SWG, CASB, ZTNA, firewall as a service
mentor.rule: SD-WAN is connectivity. SASE is SD-WAN plus the security stack, delivered from the cloud, applied wherever the user is.
mentor.tell: 'Remote and branch users must get consistent security policy without backhauling traffic to headquarters' is SASE.
mentor.trap: SD-WAN improves branch connectivity and often ships alongside security features, which blurs them. If the stem emphasises policy following the user, it is SASE.

label: Containerisation vs virtualisation, and VM escape vs container escape

mentor.diagnosis: You treated a container as a lightweight virtual machine. They isolate at different layers, which changes the blast radius.
contrast: Only the application and its dependencies
Breaking the hypervisor to reach the host or other VMs
Breaking out to the shared host kernel
Weaker, because the kernel is shared
mentor.rule: Containers share the host kernel, virtual machines do not. That single fact explains the speed advantage and the weaker isolation.
mentor.tell: 'Strong isolation is required between untrusted tenants' favours virtual machines or dedicated hosts. Density and fast startup favour containers.
mentor.trap: Containers are described as isolated, and they are, at a weaker boundary. A kernel vulnerability affects every container on the host at once.

mentor.diagnosis: You expected one device to cover the whole outage. They cover different parts of it and are designed to be used together.
contrast: Ride through a brief dip, or bridge to the generator
Sustain the site through a long outage
mentor.rule: The UPS covers the seconds the generator needs to start. Neither alone covers a long outage without interruption.
mentor.tell: 'No interruption at all, even momentarily' means a UPS must be present. 'Keep running for two days' means a generator.
mentor.trap: A generator sounds like the complete answer because it lasts far longer. It cannot start instantly, so without a UPS everything still drops.

label: Jump server vs proxy server vs reverse proxy

mentor.diagnosis: You chose an intermediary device that faces the wrong direction for the scenario.
contrast: A single hardened, monitored entry point into a protected zone
Filtering, caching and logging outbound web traffic
Fronting internal servers, TLS termination, hiding the origin
Distributing requests across a pool for capacity
mentor.rule: Jump server is for administrators entering. Forward proxy is for users leaving. Reverse proxy is for the public arriving.
mentor.tell: 'All administrative access to the production segment must pass through one auditable host' is a jump server, sometimes called a bastion host.
mentor.trap: Every one of these sits in the middle of a connection, so all four read as plausible. Identify who is initiating and in which direction.

mentor.diagnosis: You chose a failure mode without asking whether availability or security matters more for that specific system.
contrast: A door that must release in a fire, a non-critical inspection point
A firewall, a vault door, a payment segment
Fail-safe in the life safety sense
Terminology varies by context, so read the scenario
mentor.rule: Fail-closed protects data and risks an outage. Fail-open protects availability and risks exposure. Life safety almost always overrides security: doors release.
mentor.tell: 'Personnel must be able to evacuate during a power failure' means fail-open, regardless of how sensitive the area is.
mentor.trap: Fail-closed reads as the responsible security answer everywhere, and applied to an exit door it kills people. Check whether human safety is in scope.

label: Air gap vs logical segmentation vs microsegmentation

mentor.diagnosis: You called a VLAN an air gap, or proposed an air gap where the system genuinely needs connectivity.
contrast: Physical: no network connection at all
Removable media, or someone quietly adding a link
VLANs and ACLs on shared hardware
Policy per workload, often software defined
mentor.rule: An air gap means no connection exists. If data still has to move, it is not an air gap, whatever the design document calls it.
mentor.tell: 'The system must never touch the corporate network under any circumstances' is an air gap. 'Must be reachable only by the SCADA management server' is segmentation.
mentor.trap: Air gaps degrade quietly in practice. The moment someone adds a management link or walks a USB drive across, the protection is gone, and the design still claims it.
